t:
Effective on the first day of the first month following date of enactment, the basic per annum compensation of the Captain, Capitol Police force shall be $4,260: the basic per annum compensation of Lieutenants and Special Officers, Capitol Police force shall be $3,480 each; and the basic per annum compensation of Sergeants, Capitol Police force shall be $2,880 each. Effective on the first day of the first month following enactment of H.R. 15857, Eighty-ninth Congress, or similar legislation, amending the District of Columbia Police and Fireman’s Salary Act of 1958, the basic per annum compensation of the Captain, Capitol Police force shall be $4,320; the basic per annum compensation of Lieutenants and Special Officers, Capitol Police force shall be $3,600 each; and the basic per annum compensation of Sergeants, Capitol Police force shall be $2,940 each.
This Act may be cited as the “Legislative Branch Appropriation Act, 1967”.

fable.w: The section only fixes salary levels for Capitol Police officers and supplies the Act's short title. It involves no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government. The reference to enactment of other legislation is a trigger for a pay change, not an outside-party process.
fable.s: the basic per annum compensation of the Captain, Capitol Police force shall be $4,260

qwen_block.w: This section sets the salary levels for specific ranks within the Capitol Police force. It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or decision-making process involving parties outside the federal government. The actors involved are federal employees (police officers) and the legislative branch setting their pay, which is an internal government matter.

The mention of future legislation (H.R. 15857) is a congressional action, which is inside the federal government, so it is not outside participation. Nothing in the section has the government consult anyone outside it, hold a hearing or comment period, issue rules, or let outside parties sue.

It doesn't: that is Congress acting through its own legislation, which stays inside the federal government. No one outside the government is consulted, and there is no hearing, comment period, rulemaking, or right to sue.
